title: Reliable Home Heating Act
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was reported to the Senate on May 20, 2014. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Reliable Home Heating Act - Directs the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) to recognize any 30-day emergency period declared by a state governor due to a shortage of residential heating fuel (and up to two additional 30-day periods) as one during which FMCSA federal motor carrier safety regulations shall not apply to any motor carrier or driver operating a commercial motor vehicle providing residential heating fuel in a geographic area designated as under a state of emergency.

Defines the term "residential heating fuel" to include heating oil, natural gas, and propane.

Directs the Administrator of the Energy Information Administration, using data compiled from the Administration's Weekly Petroleum Status Reports, to notify the governor of each state in a Petroleum Administration for Defense District if that district's inventory of residential heating fuel has been below the most recent five-year average for more than three consecutive weeks.

Directs the Secretary of Transportation (DOT) to study the impacts on safety from the extension of exemptions issued by the state governors.

summary.headline: This law lets trucks hauling home heating fuel skip federal trucking safety rules during governor-declared fuel shortage emergencies, and tracks regional fuel supplies.
summary.what_it_does: During a state emergency declared by a governor over a shortage of home heating fuel, federal motor carrier safety rules would not apply to trucks and drivers delivering heating oil, natural gas, or propane in the affected area. The exemption covers one 30-day emergency period plus up to two more 30-day extensions. The Energy Information Administration must warn a state's governor when a regional fuel supply stays below its five-year average for more than three weeks in a row. The Department of Transportation must also study the safety effects of these exemptions.

who_it_affects.group: Truck drivers delivering home heating fuel
who_it_affects.how: During a qualifying governor-declared emergency, they would not have to follow federal motor carrier safety regulations while making deliveries in the affected area.

who_it_affects.group: Motor carriers that haul heating oil, natural gas, or propane
who_it_affects.how: Their trucks would be exempt from federal motor carrier safety rules in the emergency area during a qualifying emergency period.

who_it_affects.group: Households that heat their homes with oil, natural gas, or propane
who_it_affects.how: Fuel deliveries could move faster into areas facing shortages during a declared emergency, and state officials would get early warning when regional supplies run low.
They would receive notice from the federal government when their region's heating fuel supply is below the five-year average for an extended period, and they control whether an emergency is declared.

who_it_affects.group: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration and Department of Transportation
who_it_affects.how: The agency must recognize these emergency exemptions, and the department must study their effect on safety.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The official summary does not state an effective date; the law was enacted on June 30, 2014.
